So I'm sure the answer is really obvious, but I've never understood how manual cars really work. I get the gist of it and have been driving them for quite a while, but I've just never understood why you couldn't just pull up to a stop and keep your foot on the break without it stalling. It doesn't help either that everyone I know is either a mechanic or doesn't drive manual themselves.
ELIG - Why do you have to keep the clutch in when your manual car is stopped?

picture there is a pipe turning inside the car, and that this is the driving force of the car. the way manual transmissions work is by having the "teeth" of each different gear grip the moving pipe when you shift to them, which are in turn connected to the wheels to make it go. The clutch puts the car into neutral, in that no teeth are gripping. When you stop, you aren't applying any power to the moving pipe so the teeth gripping it will stop the momentum and cause it to stop turning, which results in the car stalling.
Maaaahhhh That actually makes sense to me. Thanks!

When you are in gear, the engine is connected to the wheels. That isn't a problem if the wheels are moving. If the wheels are not moving, the connection from the wheels to the engine will force the engine to stop.

The clutch splits the connection between the engine and the wheels.

If anyone has ever heard of Trulite, it's a glass company. Well, I applied to them and I was told it would be hot, I live in the south for reference. I thought to my self that that's okay if it's hot I'll manage. I have done landscaping in Louisiana before so the heat isn't new to me. The problem came when they issued the PPE to me. PPE means personal protection equipment or something like that. Well, it consisted of a Kevlar turtleneck sweater, a Kevlar apron, hard hat and steel toed boots and TWO pairs of gloves to wear at the same time, one a liner and the other a very thick pair of rubber gloves. The problem was the sweater. The factories average temperature was never below 100 degrees and after physically lifting large panes of glass by the hundreds and not being able to sweat because you're literally covered from head to toe in heavy clothing for 8 hours just proved too much for $12 an hour. I hate that I quit, but it was just too much. It was like when you walked in the timer started. You were fine for the first hour, hot and uncomfortable yeah, but fine. Then the second hour came and the third. By the fourth hour you're thinking about how much water you've already drank and the fact that your safety glasses are covered in so much sweat you can't really see through it. Then the heat headache kicks in. Then you finally get to go on break. You take off the big ass sweater and sit in the lightly air conditioned break room and focus on cooling off for the short 15 minutes you have. Then, you stand up and pull the big ass kevlar sweater back on slide both gloves back on and walk back to the line again.

The shifts were 8 or 12 hours. It was too much.
Just quit the hardest job I've ever done.

That's how I ended up in the Navy. Graduated from High School went to work for Echlin Manufacturing making brake parts for NAPA Auto Parts. I worked in the molding room, making rubber seals and gaskets. This was in northern Illinois during the summer. Temperature was high 80's to low 90's outside an the molds were 190 degrees and you had to spray them with a silicon and water mixture, so the humidity was 100%. We were all eating speed (white crosstops. . .) and trying to exceed our quota to get bonuses. I lasted about a month and said fuck it, the Navy is looking pretty good at this point. Good luck finding meaningful employment. Bomb disposal is fun. . .

I'm a work ethic oriented guy so I would never slow down, but everyone who was there for longer than a few months went at a survivable speed that was basically just fast enough to not get noticed by a supervisor. I prefer to go full blast and get the job done, but it's basically impossible. Our sheets of glass are like 30 feet by 10 feet or something like that and they get cut up by a machine then come down the line and we place them on dollies or on harp racks, it was back breaking doing 80+ sheets a shift. Some of them were over an inch thick so we had to work in groups just to pick them up off the line. After you blast through with adrenaline or whatever is fueling you, you look back up with your arms aching and they're still rolling down the line same speed and it just I don't know, it was just too much.
How long did you work there for? I can't imagine staying at that job for more than 2 weeks. That sounds downright awful.
About a week. That was all I could really handle and working as a pizza delivery driver during my time off was wayyyy too much.
Glad you got out of there quick. $12/hour for that kind of work is definitely NOT worth it, I think.

I feel like that's the kinda job where if you hear about it you think "oh yeah I can totally handle it" but then you go in and you just fill up with regret.

Still, I imagine it was a interesting job though? Seeing how glass is made and all.
